atoms.b: Metals are some of the ((++hardest softest)) and ((++strongest weakest)) materials around. That is why large machines, for example cranes and ships, are made of metal. This makes them strong enough to carry ((++heavy light)) loads.

Metals are also good conductors of heat. This means that heat passes through them easily, so they ((++warm_up dissolve)) and ((++cool_down glow)) quickly. That’s why ((++cooking_pots chairs)), pans and ((++baking_trays lunch_boxes)) are made of metal.

atoms.a: Iron is a silvery-grey metal. When it comes into contact with moisture in the air, a brownish layer forms on its surface. This is called rust.

atoms.b: Metals such as iron are found naturally combined with ((++rock plastic)). This combination of rock and iron is called an ore. To extract the metal from the ore, it must be heated to a very high ((++temperature height)) in an oven called a furnace.

Some particularly valuable metals such as gold, platinum and ((++silver tin)) naturally occur in ((++pure fake)) form. They can be found as small lumps in other rocks. These lumps are also known as nuggets.

atoms.a: Gold is a shiny, yellowish metal. Unlike iron, it doesn’t rust. It is comparatively rare, and therefore valuable. Gold is often used to make jewellery.
Copper is a shiny, reddish metal. It is malleable, which means it is easily shaped. This makes it a good choice of material for the pipes needed in heaters and to carry drinking water.

atoms.b: All metals conduct electricity. Because ((++copper rubber)) is relatively cheap and very ((++malleable rusty)), it is often used to make ((++electrical_wires rope)).
